notes.text: There arose a new king (after several successions in Joseph's time) which knew not Joseph — All that knew him loved him, and were kind to his relations for his sake; but when he was dead he was soon forgotten, and the remembrance of the good offices he had done was either not retained or not regarded. If we work for men only, our works at farthest will die with us; if for God, they will follow us, Rev. xiv, 13.

Come on, let us deal wisely with them, lest they multiply — When men deal wickedly it is common for them to imagine that they deal wisely, but the folly of sin will at last be manifested before all men.

They set over them task-masters, to afflict them — With this very design. They not only made them serve, which was sufficient for Pharaoh's profit, but they made them serve with rigor, so that their lives became bitter to them; intending hereby to break their spirits, and to rob them of every thing in them that was generous: to ruin their health, and shorten their days, and so diminish their numbers: to discourage them from marrying, since their children would be born to slavery; and to oblige them to desert the Hebrews, and incorporate with the Egyptians. And 'tis to be feared the oppression they were under did bring over many of them to join with the Egyptians in their idolatrous worship; for we read, Josh. xxiv, 14, that they served other gods in Egypt; and we find, Ezek. xx, 8, that God had threatned to destroy them for it, even while they were in the land of Egypt. Treasure-cities - To keep the king's money or corn, wherein a great part of the riches of Egypt consisted.

But the more they afflicted them, the more they multiplied — To the grief and vexation of the Egyptians. Times of affliction, have oft been the church's growing times: Christianity spread most when it was persecuted.

And the king spake to the Hebrew midwives — The two chief of them. They are called Hebrew midwives, probably not because they were themselves Hebrews; for sure Pharaoh could never expect they should be so barbarous to those of their own nation, but because they were generally made use of by the Hebrews, and being Egyptians he hoped to prevail with them.
The stools — Seats used on that occasion.
But the midwives feared God — Dreaded his wrath more than Pharaoh's, and therefore saved the men-children alive.

I see no reason we have to doubt the truth of this; it is plain they were now under an extraordinary blessing of increase, which may well be supposed to have this effect, that the women had quick and easy labour, and the mothers and children being both lively, they seldon needed the help of midwives; this these midwives took notice of, and concluding it to be the finger of God, were thereby emboldened to disobey the king, and with this justify themselves before Pharaoh, when he called them to an account for it.

Therefore God dealt well with them — That is, built them up in families, and blessed their children. This chapter begins the story of Moses, the most remarkable type of Christ as prophet, saviour, law-giver, and mediator, in all the Old Testament. In this chapter we have, I. The perils of his birth and infancy, ver. 1-4. II. His preservation through those perils, and the preferment of his childhood and youth, ver. 5-10. III. The pious choice of his riper years, which was to own the people of God, (1.) He offered them his service, so they would have accepted it, ver. 11-14. (2.) He retired, that he might reserve himself for farther service, ver. 15-22. IV. The dawning of the day of Israel's deliverance, ver. 23-25.
And there went a man — Amram, from the place of his abode to another place. A daughter - That is, grand-daughter of Levi.

Bare a son — It seems just at the time of his birth that cruel law was made for the murder of all the male-children of the Hebrews, and many no doubt perished by the execution of it. Moses's parents had Miriam and Aaron, both elder than he, born to them before that edict came out. Probably his mother had little joy of her being with child of him, now this edict was in force. Yet this child proves the glory of his father's house. Observe the beauty of providence: just when Pharaoh's cruelty rose to this height, the deliverer was born. She hid him three months - In some private apartment of their own house, though probably with the hazard of their lives had he been discovered. It is said, Heb. xi, 23. That Moses's parents hid him by faith: some think they had a special Revelation that the deliverer should spring from their loins; however, they believed the general promise of Israel's preservation, and in that faith hid their child.

And when she could no longer hide him, she put him in an ark of bulrushes — By the river side. God put it into their hearts to do this, to bring about his own purposes: that Moses might by this means be brought into the hands of Pharaoh's daughter, and that by his deliverance, a specimen might be given of the deliverance of God's church.

And the daughter of Pharaoh came — Providence brings no less a person than Pharaoh's daughter just at that juncture, guides her to the place where this poor infant lay, inclines her heart to pity it, which she dares do, when none else durst. Never did poor child cry so seasonably, as this did; the babe wept, which moved her compassion, as no doubt his beauty did.

And he became her son — The tradition of the Jews is, that Pharaoh's daughter had no child of her own, and that she was the only child of her father, so that when he was adopted for her son, he stood fair for the crown: however, it is certain he stood fair for the best preferments of the court in due time, and in the mean time had the advantage of the best education, with the help of which, he became master of all the lawful learning of the Egyptians Acts vii, 22. Those whom God designs for great services he finds out ways for to qualify them. Moses, by having his education in a court, is the fitter to be a prince, and king in Jeshurun; by having his education in a learned court, (for such the Egyptian then was) is the fitter to be an historian; and by having his education in the court of Egypt, is the fitter to be employed as an ambassador to that court in God's name. The Jews tell us, that his father at his circumcision called him Joachim, but Pharaoh's daughter called him Moses, Drawn out of the water, so it signifies in the Egyptian language, The calling of the Jewish lawgiver by an Egyptian name is a happy omen to the Gentile world, and gives hopes of that day when it should be said, Blessed be Egypt my people, Isaiah xix, 25. And his tuition at court was an earnest of the performance of that promise, Isaiah xlix, 23. Kings shall be thy nursing fathers, and queens thy nursing mothers.

glossa.text:
*Meanwhile there arose a new king over Egypt,* etc. ((ORIG.)) *Allegorically.* This is the devil, who *said in his heart: There is no God;* who says to his own nation, that is, to the apostate angels: *Behold the people of the children of Israel,* those, namely, who are able to see God with the mind, is mightier than we: *Come, let us oppress them wisely.* The devil perceives that the people of Israel is great, and stronger than himself, because he has often engaged them and is often overcome. He knows that Jacob wrestled, and by the help of an angel prevailed against his adversary, and was strong with God. He has felt the wrestlings of the other saints also, he has endured spiritual contests: he fears lest at some time war befall, and they consent to his adversaries, and, these being overcome [devicto eo], depart out of his land. It seems to me, from those things which had been shown to the patriarchs and prophets concerning the coming of Christ, that he perceives that One will come who will strip off his principalities and powers, and with confidence triumph over them and afflict them on the wood of the cross.

((RAB. in Exod., tom. II.)) In the Chronicles of Eusebius and Jerome we read, etc., *as far as* and he perished in the Red Sea; there were many Pharaohs.

*((ORIG. homil. 1.)) Morally.* First I wish to enquire who is the king in Egypt who knows Joseph, and who is he that knows him not. For while he was reigning who knew Joseph, the children of Israel are not said to be afflicted, nor consumed in clay and brick; nor were their males slain and their females kept alive; but only when he began to reign who had not known Joseph. If the Lord rules us, and the sense of our mind or soul is enlightened by God, remembering that Christ has risen from the dead, then in Egypt, that is, in our flesh, our spirit holds the kingdom with justice, and does not consume the children of Israel, that is, the rational senses or the virtues, in clay and brick, nor wear them away with earthly cares. If our sense should lose the memory of these things, and should not know Christ, then the wisdom of the flesh, which is an enemy to God, succeeds to the kingdom; it addresses its own nation, that is, the bodily pleasures, and, the leaders of the vices being called to council, deliberates against the children of Israel, how they may be circumvented, oppressed with clay, and afflicted with brick; how the Egyptians may expose the males, rear the females, and build cities and fortified cities. Nor is it to be thought that the divine books relate the deeds of the Egyptians without cause; but *the things that were written were written for our instruction ((Rom. XV))*, so that thou who hearest these things, if perchance thou hast been baptized and numbered among the children of Israel, and hast received the Lord as king within thee, and after this hast willed to turn aside and to do the works of the world, to perform the doings of earth and to fulfil the offices of clay: know that there has arisen in thee another king, who knows not Joseph, the king of Egypt; he himself compels thee to his own works, to labour at brick and clay; he himself, with taskmasters and drivers set over thee, drives thee with scourges to earthly works, that thou mayest build him cities; he makes thee run about through the world and, out of covetousness, throw into confusion the elements of sea and of land; to beat upon the court with lawsuits and to weary thy kinsmen with quarrels over a scanty clod of earth; to lie in wait against chastity, to deceive innocence, to commit things foul at home, cruel abroad, and shameful within the conscience: in things of this kind know that thou art soldiering for the king of Egypt, which is to be driven by the spirit of this world.

*He set therefore over them,* etc. ((ORIG.)) The devil, having called together his own nation, desires to oppress the rational sense, which is now figuratively called Israel: he sets over them masters of works, who may compel them to learn the works of the flesh, according to that of Psalm CV: *They were mingled among the heathen, and learned their works.* He teaches them to build cities for Pharaoh: Phithom, which signifies *the mouth of failing,* or *of the abyss;* and Ramesses, which is *the commotion of the moth,* and On, that is, Heliopolis, which is called the city of the sun. The mouth fails when it speaks a lie apart from truth and from proofs. He was a liar from the beginning, and therefore he wills such cities to be built for himself: *the mouth of the abyss,* because the abyss of perdition is his place; his other city is *the commotion of the moth:* for he who follows him lays up treasure there where the moth destroys, and thieves dig through and steal ((Matth. VI)). He builds also the City of the Sun, under a false name *transfiguring himself into an angel of light.* In these he occupies the minds which were made to see God. Yet he foresees that wars threaten him and the ripe destruction of his nation; therefore he says, The nation of Israel prevails over us, would that it might also perceive that we prevail over it: that is to say, that I may not receive the thoughts and the evil concupiscences which he sends in, but may repel the fiery darts with the shield of faith, and in all things that he shall suggest may say: *Get thee behind me, Satan: for it is written: Thou shalt adore the Lord thy God, and him only shalt thou serve ((Matth. IV))*. But this also which he says, Lest perchance war befall us, and these consent with our adversaries — out of the prophetic voices he foresees that war will come upon him, and that he will be forsaken by the children of Israel, and that they will consent to his adversary and be added to the Lord. This is what Jeremias says ((cap. XVII)). *The partridge has cried out, she has gathered what she did not bring forth, she has made riches, and not in judgment: in the midst of his days they shall forsake him, and in his last days he shall be a fool.* He understands therefore that he himself is the partridge who gathered what she did not bring forth; and that those whom he gathered without judgment will forsake him and will follow Christ, who begot them. He himself will remain a fool, when the whole creation shall have fled for refuge to its Maker and Parent; therefore he is indignant, saying: Lest they that fight against us go forth out of our land. He does not wish us to go out of his land, that we may always bear the image of the earthly: lest, having left him, we flee to him who has prepared the kingdom of heaven, leaving the image of the earthly and taking up the image of the heavenly. Therefore he appoints masters of works, who may teach his arts and make us craftsmen of malice. And because there are many masters of malice whom Pharaoh has set over us, who command, exact, and extort earthly works: therefore, when Christ came, he made other teachers fighting against them, who, subjecting all their principalities and powers and virtues, might defend the children of Israel from violence, and might teach them Israelite works, and to see God with the mind; to leave the works of Pharaoh, to go out of the land of Egypt, to put off Egyptian manners and the whole old man with his deeds, and to put on the new, who is created according to God.

((ISID.)) Israel signifies the Christian people, Pharaoh the devil: who lays upon them the most grievous yoke of clay and brick, that is, the servitude of earthly and miry work; with straw mingled in, that is, with light and irrational deeds: so that, all being oppressed by the burden of sins, there may be none to destroy or to overcome his kingdom.

*And the king of Egypt spoke to the midwives,* etc. ((ORIG., hom. 2.)) These things we detect not only in the world, which is spiritually called Egypt, but in each one of us: the prince of this world does not wish the males to be kept alive, but the females; by the female the flesh and the affection of the flesh is designated; but the man is the rational sense, and the intellectual spirit, which can lay hold of heavenly things, understand God, and seek the things that are above. Him the prince of Egypt hates and desires to slay; but he desires that the things which are of the flesh should live, and that those which pertain to bodily matter should not only live but be increased and cultivated: for he wills that all should savour of carnal things, should seek things temporal and those that are upon the earth; that no one should lift up his eyes to heaven; that no one should ask whence he came hither; that no one should remember paradise his fatherland. When therefore thou shalt see men leading their life in pleasures, floating in luxury, giving their labour to banquets and unchastities, know that in these the king of Egypt slays the males and keeps the females alive. But if thou see one of a thousand turned to God, lifting his eyes upward, seeking things eternal, hating delights and luxury, loving continence: him, as a male, Pharaoh desires to slay, persecutes, and assails with a thousand engines; such men he hates, he does not suffer them to live in Egypt. Hence it is that in this world the servants of God are held in contempt, exposed to insults; hence hatreds and persecutions are stirred up against them.


*To the midwives. [n: (ORIG., ibid.)]* He strives also to corrupt the midwives. *Of whom one was called Sephora,* [0186D] that is, *sparrow; the other Phua,* namely, *ruddy* or *modest;* through these he seeks that the males be slain and the females kept alive: but the midwives feared God, and did not do as he had commanded them. The midwives have taught us, before our time, to hold a certain form of rational instruction. For midwives are physicians, and they cherish both males and females at their birth. Instruction therefore is the common rational knowledge, and it reaches almost every understanding, it instructs all and cherishes all. If anyone in it be of manly spirit, one who would seek heavenly things and follow after things divine, he would come, as one healed and made strong, the readier through these instructions to the understanding of things divine. For one of them is, as it were, a *sparrow,* which teaches loftier things and calls upward on the wings of rational teaching; [0187A] *the other, ruddy* or *modest,* is moral, it composes manners, teaches modesty and honourableness. To me, however (since Scripture says of them that *they feared God, and did not act according to the precept of the king of Egypt* ), they seem to preserve the figure of both Testaments, and Sephora, who is interpreted *sparrow,* to suit the law, which is spiritual; but Phua, who is *ruddy* or *modest,* to indicate the Gospels, which are red with the blood of Christ and glow throughout the whole world with the gore of the passion. By these, therefore, the souls that are born in the Church are tended as by midwives, because from the Scriptures all the medicines of instruction are supplied. Yet Pharaoh attempts through these to slay the males, when he suggests heresies and depraved doctrines to those who are studious in the divine Scriptures. But the foundation of God stands [0187B] unmoved. For the midwives fear God, that is, they teach the fear of God, which is the beginning of wisdom. Thus what follows is the more fittingly adapted, that because the midwives feared God, they made themselves houses. Which according to the letter has no consequence: for a house is not made for the reason that God is feared. But if thou see how the Scriptures of the New and the Old Testament, teaching the fear of God, make houses for the Church, and fill the whole world with houses of prayer, it will seem reasonably written. Thus therefore these midwives, because they fear God, that is, teach the fear of God, do not do the precept of the king of Egypt, but keep the males alive; nor yet is it said that they obeyed by keeping the females alive. But I say confidently, they do not keep the females alive. For neither are vices nor [0187C] luxury taught in the Church, nor are sins nourished, which is what Pharaoh wishes when he bids the females be kept alive; but virtue alone is cultivated and nourished. But let us refer these things to each single person. If thou fearest God, thou wilt not do the precept of the king of Egypt: for he commands that thou live in delights and covet things present; thou, if thou fearest God and dost exhibit the office of a midwife, if thou desirest to profit thine own soul, keepest the males alive, that is, thou dost heal and cherish the inner man who is in thee, and through good acts and understandings dost gain eternal life.

*If it be a male,* etc. ((ISID.)) *Allegorically.* Pharaoh bids the males be killed, the females live: so the devil, lest the strength of faith prevail, the virtues being slain, wills the vices to live, and strives to kill the strong and manly senses of the mind by which we savour of things divine, that is, reason, prudence, constancy, innocence, and faith; and that which is womanish, weak, frail and prone to vices he desires to survive, that is, ambition, violence, lust, wrathfulness, and things like these, which are the figure of women.

*Who answered,* etc. ((AUG. in Gen., tom. III.)) It is asked whether such lies are approved by divine authority, etc., *as far as* but those whose conversation is already in heaven, I do not think ought to shape their measure of speech concerning truth and falsehood by the example of the midwives.

((GREG., Moral., lib. XXXVIII, cap. 2, 3.)) A lie is above all things to be guarded against, etc., *as far as* for by sparing they endeavoured to cover the life of the infants, by lying, their own.

((AUG., in lib. de Locutionibus in Exod., tom. III.)) And because the midwives feared God, etc., *as far as* so that what is consequently set forth concerning the wages to be fixed by Laban may seem to pertain to the making of that very house.

*Pharaoh therefore commanded,* etc. ((ORIG., homil. 2.)) The Egyptians, whom Pharaoh here commanded to keep only the females alive, hated the males. For they hated the virtues, they nourished the vices. Now also the Egyptians lie in wait, if a male be born to the Hebrews, that they may slay him at once, unless they beware, keep watch, and hide him. Scripture relates that someone of the tribe of Levi begot a male, and saw that the infant was goodly and hid him. Let us not, therefore, do our justice before men, but with the door shut let us pray to our Father in secret, and let not the left hand know what the right hand does, lest it be snatched away by the Egyptians, be set upon, be drowned in the waves. If I give alms because it is the work of God, I beget a male; but if I seek praise from men, and do not hide it, it is seized by the Egyptians, it is plunged into the river, and with so much labour and so much zeal I have begotten a male for the Egyptians.

*Whatsoever is of the female ((HIERON., in Ecclesiasten., c. 3))*. Wherever in the Scriptures a woman is read of, and the frailer sex, let us transfer it to the understanding of matter. Whence Pharaoh too does not wish males to be born, but females, who are near to matter; and, on the contrary, none of the saints is related, save very rarely, to have begotten daughters. And Salphaat alone, who died in his sins, begot all daughters: Jacob is the father of one daughter, and on her account is brought into peril.

*He went out,* etc. ((RAB. in Exod., tom. II.)) Hence Josephus says: But Amram, fearing lest, being seized, he should fall under the king's anger, etc., *as far as* or to lead out, as Moses was led out of the river.

*Alleg.* The parents of Moses, whose faith and works the natural law adorned ((ID., ibid.)), *as far as* she herself also is taught to blush to worship idols.

*A man of the house,* etc. ((DIOD.)) Not without design is the father of Moses passed over: for Christ also, whose type Moses bore, is without a father.

*And seeing,* etc. ((CHRYSOST., hom. 54 in Act. apost.)). It is wonderful that not through those things which seem to be of safety, but plainly through their contraries, all things are done for us. Pharaoh ordered the boys to be cast into the river; unless the boys had been cast in, Moses would not have been saved: when he was being kept safe, he was not in honour; when he was exposed, then he was made to be in honour. A Jew threatened him, saying: *Wilt thou kill me?* and this profited him, that he might philosophize in solitude and live in safety.

*((ORIG., hom. 2.)) Allegorically.* Pharaoh's daughter is the Church gathered from the Gentiles, to whom it is said by the prophet: *Forget thy people, and thy father's house, for the king hath desired thy beauty ((Psal. XLIV))*. This, therefore, is she who went out of her father's house and came to the waters, that she might be washed from the sins which she had contracted in her father's house: and at once she took on bowels of mercy, and had pity on the infant; and she, coming to the marsh, found Moses lying exposed by his own, and caused him to be nursed. He is nursed among his own, there he passes his infancy; being made stronger, he is brought to her and is adopted as a son. Moses signifies the law. The Church, therefore, coming to the waters of baptism, received the law shut up within the tibin and smeared with bitumen. Now the tibin is a kind of covering woven out of papyrus, and formed of rods or of the bark of trees. The law therefore lay shut up within coverings of this sort, smeared with pitch and bitumen, that is, with the base and foul understandings of the Jews; it lay soiled and forgotten until the Church should come from the Gentiles and take it up out of the miry and marshy places into the halls of wisdom and the royal roofs. Yet it passes its infancy among its own: for among those who do not understand it spiritually it is little, and an infant, and has the food of sucklings; when it comes to the Church, Moses is stronger and more robust; for the veil of the letter being removed, perfect food is found in the reading of him. The wages of the nursing she receives from Pharaoh's daughter, with whom the law is born and nursed. But what is it that the Synagogue receives from the Church? I think it is that which Moses says: *I will lead you into emulation by that which is not a nation: by a foolish nation I will stir you up to wrath.* The Synagogue therefore receives this wage from the Church, that it should no longer worship idols: for seeing the Gentiles so turned to God that they no longer know idols, it blushes any longer to worship idols. We also, if we have had Pharaoh for a father, if he begot us in evil works, when we shall have come to the waters, let us take up the law of God: let not the letters be foul to us as an obscure covering; let us eat those things of it which are small and of milk; let us take up those which are perfect, and let us store them within the royal roofs of the heart. We have a great and strong Moses: let us think nothing small of him, nothing base, but all magnificent, all excellent, all elegant: for all is great that is spiritual and of a lofty understanding.

*And seeing in it a little one,* etc. ((THEOD.)) *Mystically.* This above all could betray him to her, for the Egyptians had not yet admitted such a mystery, although in a later time they observed the law of circumcision in imitation of the Hebrews. Whence Jeremias: *I will consider all that cut round the foreskin, the Egyptians and the sons of Edom. ((Jer. IX))* 

((ISID.)) Moses, that is, Christ, is found by the faithful at the river of the laver and the water of baptism, etc., *as far as* and receiving him with religious observance they guard him.

*And when he was grown she delivered him,* etc. ((RAB.)) Josephus relates that Pharaoh's daughter brought Moses, when grown, to her father, who set his own crown upon him, which Moses at once threw down, because he saw a graven image sculptured there. Whence the priest who was present wished to kill him, saying that Egypt was to be overthrown by him, as he had received from the oracle of the demons. But Pharaoh's daughter delivered him. And when he was of full age, he was sent by Pharaoh against the Ethiopians. And since he knew that he would journey through deserts full of serpents, he took ibises, that is, Egyptian storks, and, having measured out his camp, brought them forward, that they might devour the serpents and put them to flight: and thus the army passed the night in safety. When therefore he had come to the city which he was to storm, the queen of the Ethiopians fell in love with him, and according to the agreement delivered the city to him and married him: hence it is that Aaron and Mary quarrelled against Moses on account of his Ethiopian wife.

notes.text: The proud — Our enemies, compared to proud waters, for their great multitude and swelling rage. The safety of them that trust in God, and the fate of the wicked, ver. 1-5. A song of degrees.

glossa.text: *If it had not been that.* ((CASS.)) First the holy martyrs, mindful of how great things they have escaped, ascribe them to mercy alone; secondly, they give thanks that they have been delivered.

*Perhaps they had swallowed us up alive.* They live who know that an idol is nothing. They are dead who think it to be something. Therefore the dead are swallowed up, who think that the evil which they do is a thing to be done; but the living are they who indeed know that what they do is evil, but being overcome by persecution pass over into the fellowship of the ungodly, and prefer the sweetness of this life to God, as certain men did who for fear of death sacrificed to idols. ((AUG.)) Mark also that Peter, that is, the Church, swallows up many, but not alive. To whom it is said: *Slay and eat. ((Act. X.))* For he eats none, that is, sets none among his members, save one slain, that is, one renouncing the devil. He therefore is slain as to evil, but quickened as to good, who is eaten by Peter. The contrary befalls him whom the devil swallows down.

*Water.* ((AUG.)) The sinful people (and it is from the likeness of the Egyptians): which water flows as a torrent with violence, but quickly passes; whence he subjoins: *a torrent. --Perhaps* the Latins set down, as best they can, for the Greek ἄρα in the place of doubting, which is more intelligibly said: *thinkest thou, has our soul passed through?* that is, the greatness of the peril scarcely suffers this to be believed.
*Water insupportable.* ((AUG.)) Without substance, as are vices, and sins, and the sweetness of this life, etc., *as far as* and might bring back to the father the prodigal son worn out by long need.
*Blessed be the Lord.* ((CASS.)) The second part, where the saints give thanks that they have been delivered and that the snare has been broken.

*Our soul.* ((AUG.)) Or, as when someone makes a great noise, etc., *as far as* which is as it were a snare. *Of them that hunt.* ((ID.)) The hunters are the persecutors; the bait in the trap, the sweetness of this life. *The snare is broken.* ((CASS.)) The martyrs being slain, there remains no sweetness of life whereby they might be taken again: but they themselves were not broken along with it, nay rather delivered. *Broken.* ((ID.)) As if he should say: because it was of iron; not torn apart, like tow: so great was the fortitude of the passion, so great the power of him that delivered.

notes.text: I exhort you — St. Paul uses to suit his exhortations to the doctrines he has been delivering. So here the general use from the whole is contained in the first and second verses. The particular uses follow, from the third verse to the end of the Epistle. By the tender mercies of God - The whole sentiment is derived from Romans. The expression itself is particularly opposed to "the wrath of God," chap. i, 18. It has a reference here to the entire gospel, to the whole economy of grace or mercy, delivering us from "the wrath of God," and exciting us to all duty. To present - So chap. vi, 13; xvi, 19; now actually to exhibit before God. Your bodies - That is, yourselves; a part is put for the whole; the rather, as in the ancient sacrifices of beasts, the body was the whole. These also are particularly named in opposition to that vile abuse of their bodies mentioned, chap. i, 24. Several expressions follow, which have likewise a direct reference to other expressions in the same chapter. A sacrifice - Dead to sin and living - By that life which is mentioned, chap. i, 17; vi, 4, &c. Holy - Such as the holy law requires, chap. vii, 12. Acceptable - chap. viii, 8. Which is your reasonable service - The worship of the heathens was utterly unreasonable, chap. i, 18, &c.; so was the glorying of the Jews, chap. ii, 3, &c. But a Christian acts in all things by the highest reason, from the mercy of God inferring his own duty.

And be not conformed — Neither in judgment, spirit, nor behaviour. To this world - Which, neglecting the will of God, entirely follows its own. That ye may prove - Know by sure trial; which is easily done by him who has thus presented himself to God. What is that good, and acceptable, and perfect will of God - The will of God is here to be understood of all the preceptive part of Christianity, which is in itself so excellently good, so acceptable to God, and so perfective of our natures.

And I say — He now proceeds to show what that will of God is. Through the grace which is given to me - He modestly adds this, lest he should seem to forget his own direction. To every one that is among you - Believers at Rome. Happy, had they always remembered this! The measure of faith - Treated of in the first and following chapters, from which all other gifts and graces flow.
So we — All believers. Are one body - Closely connected together in Christ, and consequently ought to be helpful to each other.

Having then gifts differing according to the grace which is given us — Gifts are various: grace is one. Whether it be prophecy - This, considered as an extraordinary gift, is that whereby heavenly mysteries are declared to men, or things to come foretold. But it seems here to mean the ordinary gift of expounding scripture. Let us prophesy according to the analogy of faith - St. Peter expresses it, "as the oracles of God;" according to the general tenor of them; according to that grand scheme of doctrine which is delivered therein, touching original sin, justification by faith, and present, inward salvation. There is a wonderful analogy between all these; and a close and intimate connection between the chief heads of that faith "which was once delivered to the saints." Every article therefore concerning which there is any question should be determined by this rule; every doubtful scripture interpreted according to the grand truths which run through the whole.

Ministering — As deacons. He that teacheth - Catechumens; for whom particular instructers were appointed. He that exhorteth - Whose peculiar business it was to urge Christians to duty, and to comfort them in trials.
He that presideth — That hath the care of a flock. He that showeth mercy - In any instance. With cheerfulness - Rejoicing that he hath such an opportunity.

glossa.text:
*I beseech you.* Thus far he has sufficiently humbled both parties, and has annulled the glory drawn from their former state; now, the business being as it were finished, he thereafter turns to morality. *I beseech you.* Thus far, lest the one should be proud against the other; from here, that the one should labor for the other's profit. *I beseech you by,* etc. That is, by the apostolate mercifully committed to me by God, or the mercy wrought and shown to you by God.

*A victim,* etc. ((AUG., lib. X, de Civit., cap. 6.)) A true sacrifice is every work that is done, etc, *as far as* he adds, saying: *But be ye reformed in the newness of your mind,* etc.

*Be not conformed.* A general prohibition. *But be ye reformed.* A regular command. There continence, here justice. The one pertains to not coveting, this to loving; the one to turning aside from evil, this to doing good. For by not coveting we are stripped of the oldness, and by loving we are clothed with the newness. *Be ye reformed.* Because in Adam the image of God was in part lost, so that it may begin to be reformed by him by whom it was formed. For it cannot reform itself as it was able to deform itself.

*For I say.* This is the sacrifice of Christians, that the many should be one body in Christ. For this is shown in the Sacrament of the altar to the faithful by the vow of the Church, which is signified in that thing which she offers. For as bread is made of many grains, so the holy Church consists of the many members of the faithful, who rejoice together in the participation of their Creator; by whose gift they are holy and are one, which is also shown in what follows, where he says: *We being many are one body in Christ ((I Cor. X))*. Which cannot come to pass unless they be wise unto sobriety, which is here enjoined. *To be wise unto sobriety.* That is, that it should not go beyond the bounds of justice, that which may be useful to us alone, and may hurt no one.

 *The measure of faith.* According to the faith which God distributes by measure; this is the faith that works through charity, without which no man's works are to be reckoned anything. To Christ the Spirit was not given by measure, but to all the rest it is given, and being given is added to; whence John says of Christ: *For God doth not give the Spirit by measure,* to the rest it is divided, not indeed the Spirit, but his gifts.

*For as in one. ((AUG.))* No one will be able to be just so long as he has been separated from the unity of this body, etc., *as far as* but that they may possess them with the piety of using them well.

*And every one members one of another, having,* etc. To this end having differing goods. Or: we are severally members, therefore let this be done in the differing gifts; and what those graces are from the diversity of which we are called members, and in what manner in them we ought to serve one another in turn, he opens, saying: *Whether prophecy according to the proportion of faith, or ministry,* etc. *Having*: let us be members of others, that we may prophesy to them. I say *having according to the proportion of faith,* because prophecy is given according as their faith, or the faith of the hearers, requires. Note that in the enumeration of the graces he begins from prophecy, because the first proof that our faith is reasonable is that believers, having received the Spirit, prophesied.

*He that showeth mercy.* This showing of mercy is the daily medicine for daily wounds, even though they be the lighter ones; yet *judgment without mercy shall be done to him that doth not mercy ((Jac. II))*, and this is assuredly just, that it be forgiven to him that forgives and given to him that gives. But whosoever, as being over-just and secure, awaits judgment without mercy, provokes wrath against himself. This mercy is manifold, namely to pardon him that sins, to succor him that is oppressed, etc.; and therefore he subjoins concerning mercy, setting down one member of it when another member has been set before, but where *he that giveth, in simplicity.* Simplicity excludes hypocrisy, cheerfulness shows joy, and reliance upon the hope of what is to come.

notes.text: And Jesus coming — There was a large interval of time between what has been related, and what follows. The passages that follow were but a short time before our Lord suffered. Mark viii, 27; Luke ix, 18.
Jeremiah, or one of the prophets — There was at that time a current tradition among the Jews, that either Jeremiah, or some other of the ancient prophets would rise again before the Messiah came.
Peter — Who was generally the most forward to speak.
Flesh and blood — That is, thy own reason, or any natural power whatsoever.

On this rock — Alluding to his name, which signifies a rock, namely, the faith which thou hast now professed; I will build my Church - But perhaps when our Lord uttered these words, he pointed to himself, in like manner as when he said, Destroy this temple, John ii, 19; meaning the temple of his body. And it is certain, that as he is spoken of in Scripture, as the only foundation of the Church, so this is that which the apostles and evangelists laid in their preaching. It is in respect of laying this, that the names of the twelve apostles (not of St. Peter only) were equally inscribed on the twelve foundations of the city of God, Rev. xxi, 14. The gates of hell - As gates and walls were the strength of cities, and as courts of judicature were held in their gates, this phrase properly signifies the power and policy of Satan and his instruments. Shall not prevail against it - Not against the Church universal, so as to destroy it. And they never did. There hath been a small remnant in all ages.

I will give thee the keys of the kingdom of heaven — Indeed not to him alone, (for they were equally given to all the apostles at the same time, John xx, 21, 22, 23;) but to him were first given the keys both of doctrine and discipline. He first, after our Lord's resurrection, exercised the apostleship, Acts i, 15. And he first by preaching opened the kingdom of heaven, both to the Jews, Acts ii, , and to the Gentiles, Acts x, . Under the term of binding and loosing are contained all those acts of discipline which Peter and his brethren performed as apostles: and undoubtedly what they thus performed on earth, God confirmed in heaven. Matt. xviii, 18.

Then charged he his disciples to tell no one that he was the Christ. Jesus himself had not said it expressly even to his apostles, but left them to infer it from his doctrine and miracles. Neither was it proper the apostles should say this openly, before that grand proof of it, his resurrection. If they had, they who believed them would the more earnestly have sought to take and make him a king: and they who did not believe them would the more vehemently have rejected and opposed such a Messiah.

glossa.text: *Into the parts of Caesarea Philippi.* This is the place where the Jordan rises at the foot of Lebanon, out of Jor and Dan, two springs. *That men say he is.* They are men who speak of the Son of man: for they are gods who understand the Godhead. *The Son of man?* The Lord professes of himself the lowliness of his humanity, while the disciples understand his Godhead.

*Some, John the Baptist.* So they could err about Elias or about the rest of the others, as Herod erred about John when he said: *John, whom I beheaded, is risen from the dead: and therefore mighty works are wrought in him ((Marc. VI))* . Therefore he wills that their errors be set forth, so that, these being driven off, the disciples may bring forth the truth, not out of the opinion of the common people, but out of the Lord's revelation.

*Simon Peter answering.* Therefore one answers, and to one answer is made on behalf of all, that unity may be kept in all. *Of the living God.* For a distinction from the false gods, which the Gentiles set up for themselves either out of dead men or out of sensible matter.

*Barjona.* Well is he the son of the dove, because he followed the Lord with a devout simplicity, or because he was full of spiritual grace. He is called the son of the Holy Spirit, who was shown in the dove, by him whom he had called the Son of the living God, and to the son of the dove the Father reveals, because the operation of the Father and of the Son with the Holy Spirit is one. He reveals, I say, the mystery of faith, because flesh and blood could not reveal it, that is, men puffed up with carnal wisdom, who are not sons of the dove, and therefore strangers to the wisdom of the Spirit; of whom above: *Others John the Baptist, and others Elias,* etc.

*Thou art.* I do not say, thou shalt be called, but thou art Peter, for the strength of thy faith and the constancy of thy confession. *Peter.* From me, the Rock, yet so that I keep for myself the dignity of the foundation: thou shalt set clean stones upon me, and shalt cast away the leprous.

Just as light and the other names, as: *You are the salt of the earth,* were allotted to the apostles by the Lord, so to Simon he gave from himself the name of Peter.

*And the gates.* The gates of hell are sins, threats, blandishments, heresies, by which the weak rush into death, who are to be believed to have built the house of their profession not truly upon the rock, but upon the sand, that is, not to follow Christ with a simple and true intention, but to have put forward the habit for some earthly cause. For he who receives the faith of Christ in the inmost love of the heart easily overcomes whatever assails him from without.

*And whatsoever thou shalt bind.* That is, whomsoever thou shalt have adjudged to eternal punishments as persisting in his sins, or whomsoever thou shalt have absolved as humble and truly penitent, so shall it be also in heaven.

*And whatsoever thou shalt bind upon earth. ((HIER.))* The other apostles have indeed the same judicial power, to whom after the resurrection he says: *Receive ye the Holy Spirit ((Joan. XX))*, etc., *as far as* whence in Leviticus the lepers are bidden to show themselves to the priests, whom the priests do not make lepers, but discern who are clean or unclean, so also here.

*That they should tell no man,* etc. Above he commands them to preach his coming, here that they should not say that he is Jesus. But it is one thing to preach Christ, which is a common name of dignity: another to preach Jesus, which is the Saviour's own name. As if he said: It does not profit that my majesty be publicly preached to the peoples, who are to see me suffer many things, which will be lawful only then, when the resurrection shall have shown the power of the Godhead. *Jesus Christ.* The Saviour: lest they should be scandalized in him whom a little after they are to see spat upon and crucified.

echoes.text: “‘If his offering is a burnt offering from the herd, he shall offer a male without defect. He shall offer it at the door of the Tent of Meeting, that he may be accepted before Yahweh. He shall lay his hand on the head of the burnt offering, and it shall be accepted for him to make atonement for him.
echoes.note: "Present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God" reuses the technical cultic vocabulary of the burnt offering, which must be presented/brought 'acceptable before the LORD' (LXX dekton). Paul figurally transposes the Levitical offering from animal victim to the embodied self.

echoes.text: For you don’t delight in sacrifice, or else I would give it. You have no pleasure in burnt offering. The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit. A broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise.
echoes.note: The Psalm's claim that God does not delight in animal sacrifice but in 'a broken spirit' anticipates Paul's redefinition of true worship (logike latreia) as the offering of the whole self rather than the slain victim.

echoes.text: Samuel said, “Has Yahweh as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of Yahweh? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams.
echoes.note: 'To obey is better than sacrifice' belongs to the prophetic stream that internalizes and ethicizes cult; Paul's 'reasonable/spiritual service' redirects sacrifice toward obedient self-presentation in the same key.

echoes.text: I will also give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you; and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh.
echoes.note: The promise of a 'new heart and a new spirit' stands behind 'be transformed by the renewing of your mind'; the eschatological interior renewal of the prophets is here applied to the believing community.

echoes.text: For I desire mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.
echoes.note: 'I desire mercy and not sacrifice' is part of the prophetic critique that grounds Paul's reframing of worship as embodied, merciful obedience rather than ritual offering.

echoes.text: How shall I come before Yahweh, and bow myself before the exalted God? Shall I come before him with burnt offerings, with calves a year old? Will Yahweh be pleased with thousands of rams? With tens of thousands of rivers of oil? Shall I give my firstborn for my disobedience? The fruit of my body for the sin of my soul? He has shown you, O man, what is good. What does Yahweh require of you, but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?
echoes.note: Micah's rhetorical rejection of burnt offerings in favor of doing justice and walking humbly parallels Paul's contrast between cultic sacrifice and 'living sacrifice' as the true service God requires.

echoes.text: But this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, says Yahweh: I will put my law in their inward parts, and in their heart will I write it; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people:
echoes.note: The new-covenant law written on the heart/mind (LXX dianoia) coheres with the 'renewing of the mind' that enables one to discern God's will; faint verbal contact via mind/heart-renewal.

echoes.text: For this commandment which I command you this day is not too hard for you or too distant. It is not in heaven, that you should say, “Who will go up for us to heaven, and bring it to us, and proclaim it to us, that we may do it?” Neither is it beyond the sea, that you should say, “Who will go over the sea for us, and bring it to us, and proclaim it to us, that we may do it?” But the word is very near to you, in your mouth and in your heart, that you may do […]
echoes.note: Discerning and doing 'the good and acceptable and perfect will of God' echoes Deuteronomy's insistence that God's commandment is knowable and doable, internalized in heart and mouth — a theme Paul invokes nearby in Romans 10.

echoes.text: Don’t be wise in your own eyes. Fear Yahweh, and depart from evil.
echoes.note: 'Not to think of himself more highly than he ought' draws on the wisdom warning 'Be not wise in your own eyes'; the same maxim returns explicitly at 12:16, framing the pericope's call to sober self-estimation.

echoes.text: Do you see a man wise in his own eyes? There is more hope for a fool than for him.
echoes.note: 'Do you see a man wise in his own conceit? There is more hope for a fool' supplies the proverbial backdrop for Paul's exhortation against inflated self-regard ('think reasonably').

echoes.text: Pride is hateful before the Lord and before men; And in the judgement of both will unrighteousness err.
echoes.note: Sirach's wisdom that 'pride is hateful before the Lord and before men' is a Second Temple parallel to Paul's call not to over-rate oneself but to measure by the faith God apportions.

echoes.text: I will lay the key of the house of David on his shoulder. He will open, and no one will shut. He will shut, and no one will open.
echoes.note: 'I will give you the keys of the Kingdom of Heaven... bind... loose' draws on the Eliakim oracle: 'I will place on his shoulder the key of the house of David; he shall open and none shut, shut and none open.' The key-of-stewardship granting authority to admit and exclude is the controlling image. Strong verbal and conceptual borrowing.

echoes.text: Have the gates of death been revealed to you? Or have you seen the gates of the shadow of death?
echoes.note: 'The gates of Hades will not prevail' echoes 'Have the gates of death been revealed to you?' — the underworld as a fortified city whose gates symbolize the realm and power of death. Verbal touchpoint ('gates' of death/Hades).

echoes.text: Have mercy on me, Yahweh. See my affliction by those who hate me, and lift me up from the gates of death;
echoes.note: 'You who lift me up from the gates of death' supplies the same 'gates of death/Hades' idiom; deliverance from death's gates is precisely what Jesus' resurrection-grounded assembly will enjoy. Reinforces Job 38:17.

echoes.text: I said, “In the middle of my life I go into the gates of Sheol. I am deprived of the residue of my years.”
echoes.note: Hezekiah's 'I shall go through the gates of Sheol' offers another close instance of the 'gates of the underworld' figure standing behind 'gates of Hades.'

echoes.text: For who is there of all flesh, that has heard the voice of the living God speaking out of the midst of the fire, as we have, and lived?
echoes.note: Peter's confession of Jesus as 'the Son of the living God' employs the covenant title 'the living God,' contrasting Israel's God with lifeless idols. The epithet recurs across the OT and grounds the confession in covenant monotheism.

echoes.text: Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of Yahweh comes.
echoes.note: The popular identification of Jesus with Elijah ('some say... Elijah') depends on Malachi's promise that Elijah would return before the day of the LORD, an expectation Matthew engages elsewhere (11:14; 17:10-13).

echoes.text: Yet the number of the children of Israel will be as the sand of the sea, which can’t be measured nor numbered; and it will come to pass that, in the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ they will be called ‘sons of the living God.’
echoes.note: 'Sons of the living God' supplies the specific collocation 'living God' with sonship language that Peter's title brings together. Faint verbal overlap.

echoes.text: “Listen to me, you who follow after righteousness, you who seek Yahweh: look to the rock you were cut from, and to the hold of the pit you were dug from. Look to Abraham your father, and to Sarah who bore you; for when he was but one I called him, and I blessed him, and made him many.
echoes.note: 'On this rock I will build' may play on the 'rock from which you were hewn' (Abraham) imagery for the founding of the people of God on a chosen progenitor. Disputed; rock-foundation imagery is diffuse.

echoes.text: “Before I formed you in the belly, I knew you. Before you came out of the womb, I sanctified you. I have appointed you a prophet to the nations.”
echoes.note: Jeremiah being named among the guesses for Jesus' identity reflects his stature as the suffering, rejected prophet of judgment on Jerusalem; the allusion is to Jeremiah as a prophetic type rather than a specific text. Faint.

notes.text: Look — Consider the state of Abraham and Sarah, from whom all of you sprang.

Him alone — To follow me to an unknown land: him only of all his kindred. Increased - Into a vast multitude, when his condition was desperate in the eye of reason. And therefore God can as easily raise his church when they are in the most forlorn condition.
Therefore — For the sake of Abraham, and of that covenant which I made with him. Garden - Flourishing as the garden of Eden.

My people — Ye Jews, whom I chose to be my peculiar people. A law - A new law, even the doctrine of the gospel. Judgment - Judgment is here the same thing with law, the word of God, or the evangelical doctrine, of which he saith that he will make it to rest, that is settle and establish it. The people - People of all nations.

My righteousness — My salvation, the redemption of all my people, Jews and Gentiles, which is the effect of his righteousness, his justice, faithfulness, or mercy. Is gone - Shall shortly go forth. Judge - Shall subdue the Gentiles to my authority, and rule them by my word and spirit. Isles - The remote countries shall expect this salvation from me, and from me only.
The heavens — The heavens and earth shall pass away, in regard of their present state, and properties, and use, as smoak is said to vanish, tho' the substance of it be not destroyed.

glossa.text:
*Hearken to me, you that follow that which.* ((HIER.)) *Look unto the rock.* Christ. Of which, *And the rock was Christ, out of which you are hewn ((I Cor. X))*, from Christ called Christians.

*And to the cavern of the pit.* On account of the digging of Christ's side, etc., *as far as* we are born through the laver of baptism.

*Joy and gladness.* Note that in Sion, which is compared to the paradise of God, there ought to be so much joy and gladness and thanksgiving and the voice of praise, that what they are to do in heaven with the angels they should meditate on continually upon earth.
*My just one.* Justifying all, or justice elegantly: not that one nation, but that the whole world may be saved.
*The heavens like smoke.* ((ID.)) It is written of the saints, etc., *as far as* yet some take "to perish" and "to grow old" for abolition and death.

notes.text: The gods — Before kings and princes.
Temple — Where the ark was. He was not permitted to enter into it. Magnified - For thou hast glorified thy word or promise unto me more than any other of thy glorious perfections.
The kings — A prophecy of the calling of the Gentiles. Hear - The gospel preached among then.
The ways — His wonderful counsel and gracious providences.

Perfect — Will finish the great work of my deliverance. Forsake not - Or, do not give over, the work of my salvation, which is thus far advanced, not by any human help, but by thy power and providence. This psalm is, by many of the Jewish doctors, esteemed the most excellent in the whole book. The omniscience of God is here asserted, ver. 1-6. Proved by two arguments; That he is everywhere present, ver. 7-12. And that he made us, ver. 13-16. This may fill us with pleasing admiration of God, ver. 17, 18. With an holy hatred of sin, ver. 19-22. And with an holy satisfaction in our own integrity, ver. 23, 24. To the chief musician, A psalm of David.

glossa.text:
*A psalm to David himself.* ((CASS.)) The captive, who had wept, as though Jerusalem and the temple were rebuilt, and as a fellow-citizen with that part of Jerusalem which was not captive, that is, with the angels, rejoices and praises first the benefits given him. In the person therefore of the Church, which is in the things above in hope, awaiting to be there in reality, he says, *I will confess.*

*I will confess to thee, O Lord.* First, he commends the benefits given him: secondly, he tells how these are spread abroad unto all, there, *Let them confess to thee, O Lord,* etc. *In the sight.* ((AUG.)) In praising I set before myself the angels, to whom I look to be made equal in dignity hereafter, as I am now. But these in the praise of God set before themselves nothing else but himself. *In the sight* therefore *of the angels,* in that purity wherein the angels behold thee, that in thee alone they may rest, I *will sing to thee.*

*For thy mercy.* ((ID.)) *All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth:* There are no other ways by which he came to us, there are no others by which we may come to him: let us render these to God, mercy in succouring, truth in judging. *Above every holy name of thine.* ((CASS.)) Or above thy holy name, when thy worship became known to us.
*In the soul.* And because in the soul a carnal multiplication can take place, he adds, *strength,* as though: I seek nothing else in the soul but strength.

*Let them confess.* ((ID.)) The second part, where it is said *dici*; read *dicit*, "he tells" how these good things are to be spread abroad unto all. As it were, after my example: *Let them confess,* etc. *All the words of thy mouth.* ((AUG.)) Which have now been revealed everywhere, and sent unto all nations, etc., *as far as* and thus, the fleece being dried, *they heard all the words,* etc.

*Great is the glory.* ((ID.)) If they are humble, they love and sing this; for if they exalt themselves, let them fear what follows. *For the Lord is high. He looketh on the low things.* ((CASS.)) Here is not the human condition, where the humble man is despised and the proud man regarded; but the Lord regards the humble.

*The high he knoweth afar off.* ((AUG.)) The proud man does not this, etc., *as far as* mourning this sojourning, whence it is subjoined.

*If I shall walk in the midst of tribulation.* Otherwise he does not quicken, save *in the midst of tribulation,* whence, *Blessed are they that mourn, woe to them that laugh.*

*Upon the wrath.* ((ID.)) This very thing, that they are angry with me, is thy chastisement upon them, that is, thy punishment. For to be angry is to them a punishment, not *noc* only a fault. While therefore thou permittest this, thou stretchest forth the hand of vengeance upon them all.

*Thy right hand.* God has not a right hand or a left, but the right hand of God is called eternal happiness, the left, temporal happiness. Sometimes therefore he does not save his saints in the left hand, but he always saves them in the right.
*He will repay.* ((AUG.)) What I cannot do, etc., *as far as* in whom the princes of the world found no sin, wherefore they should kill him.

notes.text: I exhort you — St. Paul uses to suit his exhortations to the doctrines he has been delivering. So here the general use from the whole is contained in the first and second verses. The particular uses follow, from the third verse to the end of the Epistle. By the tender mercies of God - The whole sentiment is derived from Romans. The expression itself is particularly opposed to "the wrath of God," chap. i, 18. It has a reference here to the entire gospel, to the whole economy of grace or mercy, delivering us from "the wrath of God," and exciting us to all duty. To present - So chap. vi, 13; xvi, 19; now actually to exhibit before God. Your bodies - That is, yourselves; a part is put for the whole; the rather, as in the ancient sacrifices of beasts, the body was the whole. These also are particularly named in opposition to that vile abuse of their bodies mentioned, chap. i, 24. Several expressions follow, which have likewise a direct reference to other expressions in the same chapter. A sacrifice - Dead to sin and living - By that life which is mentioned, chap. i, 17; vi, 4, &c. Holy - Such as the holy law requires, chap. vii, 12. Acceptable - chap. viii, 8. Which is your reasonable service - The worship of the heathens was utterly unreasonable, chap. i, 18, &c.; so was the glorying of the Jews, chap. ii, 3, &c. But a Christian acts in all things by the highest reason, from the mercy of God inferring his own duty.

And be not conformed — Neither in judgment, spirit, nor behaviour. To this world - Which, neglecting the will of God, entirely follows its own. That ye may prove - Know by sure trial; which is easily done by him who has thus presented himself to God. What is that good, and acceptable, and perfect will of God - The will of God is here to be understood of all the preceptive part of Christianity, which is in itself so excellently good, so acceptable to God, and so perfective of our natures.

And I say — He now proceeds to show what that will of God is. Through the grace which is given to me - He modestly adds this, lest he should seem to forget his own direction. To every one that is among you - Believers at Rome. Happy, had they always remembered this! The measure of faith - Treated of in the first and following chapters, from which all other gifts and graces flow.
So we — All believers. Are one body - Closely connected together in Christ, and consequently ought to be helpful to each other.

Having then gifts differing according to the grace which is given us — Gifts are various: grace is one. Whether it be prophecy - This, considered as an extraordinary gift, is that whereby heavenly mysteries are declared to men, or things to come foretold. But it seems here to mean the ordinary gift of expounding scripture. Let us prophesy according to the analogy of faith - St. Peter expresses it, "as the oracles of God;" according to the general tenor of them; according to that grand scheme of doctrine which is delivered therein, touching original sin, justification by faith, and present, inward salvation. There is a wonderful analogy between all these; and a close and intimate connection between the chief heads of that faith "which was once delivered to the saints." Every article therefore concerning which there is any question should be determined by this rule; every doubtful scripture interpreted according to the grand truths which run through the whole.

Ministering — As deacons. He that teacheth - Catechumens; for whom particular instructers were appointed. He that exhorteth - Whose peculiar business it was to urge Christians to duty, and to comfort them in trials.
He that presideth — That hath the care of a flock. He that showeth mercy - In any instance. With cheerfulness - Rejoicing that he hath such an opportunity.

glossa.text:
*I beseech you.* Thus far he has sufficiently humbled both parties, and has annulled the glory drawn from their former state; now, the business being as it were finished, he thereafter turns to morality. *I beseech you.* Thus far, lest the one should be proud against the other; from here, that the one should labor for the other's profit. *I beseech you by,* etc. That is, by the apostolate mercifully committed to me by God, or the mercy wrought and shown to you by God.

*A victim,* etc. ((AUG., lib. X, de Civit., cap. 6.)) A true sacrifice is every work that is done, etc, *as far as* he adds, saying: *But be ye reformed in the newness of your mind,* etc.

*Be not conformed.* A general prohibition. *But be ye reformed.* A regular command. There continence, here justice. The one pertains to not coveting, this to loving; the one to turning aside from evil, this to doing good. For by not coveting we are stripped of the oldness, and by loving we are clothed with the newness. *Be ye reformed.* Because in Adam the image of God was in part lost, so that it may begin to be reformed by him by whom it was formed. For it cannot reform itself as it was able to deform itself.

*For I say.* This is the sacrifice of Christians, that the many should be one body in Christ. For this is shown in the Sacrament of the altar to the faithful by the vow of the Church, which is signified in that thing which she offers. For as bread is made of many grains, so the holy Church consists of the many members of the faithful, who rejoice together in the participation of their Creator; by whose gift they are holy and are one, which is also shown in what follows, where he says: *We being many are one body in Christ ((I Cor. X))*. Which cannot come to pass unless they be wise unto sobriety, which is here enjoined. *To be wise unto sobriety.* That is, that it should not go beyond the bounds of justice, that which may be useful to us alone, and may hurt no one.

 *The measure of faith.* According to the faith which God distributes by measure; this is the faith that works through charity, without which no man's works are to be reckoned anything. To Christ the Spirit was not given by measure, but to all the rest it is given, and being given is added to; whence John says of Christ: *For God doth not give the Spirit by measure,* to the rest it is divided, not indeed the Spirit, but his gifts.

*For as in one. ((AUG.))* No one will be able to be just so long as he has been separated from the unity of this body, etc., *as far as* but that they may possess them with the piety of using them well.

*And every one members one of another, having,* etc. To this end having differing goods. Or: we are severally members, therefore let this be done in the differing gifts; and what those graces are from the diversity of which we are called members, and in what manner in them we ought to serve one another in turn, he opens, saying: *Whether prophecy according to the proportion of faith, or ministry,* etc. *Having*: let us be members of others, that we may prophesy to them. I say *having according to the proportion of faith,* because prophecy is given according as their faith, or the faith of the hearers, requires. Note that in the enumeration of the graces he begins from prophecy, because the first proof that our faith is reasonable is that believers, having received the Spirit, prophesied.

*He that showeth mercy.* This showing of mercy is the daily medicine for daily wounds, even though they be the lighter ones; yet *judgment without mercy shall be done to him that doth not mercy ((Jac. II))*, and this is assuredly just, that it be forgiven to him that forgives and given to him that gives. But whosoever, as being over-just and secure, awaits judgment without mercy, provokes wrath against himself. This mercy is manifold, namely to pardon him that sins, to succor him that is oppressed, etc.; and therefore he subjoins concerning mercy, setting down one member of it when another member has been set before, but where *he that giveth, in simplicity.* Simplicity excludes hypocrisy, cheerfulness shows joy, and reliance upon the hope of what is to come.

notes.text: And Jesus coming — There was a large interval of time between what has been related, and what follows. The passages that follow were but a short time before our Lord suffered. Mark viii, 27; Luke ix, 18.
Jeremiah, or one of the prophets — There was at that time a current tradition among the Jews, that either Jeremiah, or some other of the ancient prophets would rise again before the Messiah came.
Peter — Who was generally the most forward to speak.
Flesh and blood — That is, thy own reason, or any natural power whatsoever.

On this rock — Alluding to his name, which signifies a rock, namely, the faith which thou hast now professed; I will build my Church - But perhaps when our Lord uttered these words, he pointed to himself, in like manner as when he said, Destroy this temple, John ii, 19; meaning the temple of his body. And it is certain, that as he is spoken of in Scripture, as the only foundation of the Church, so this is that which the apostles and evangelists laid in their preaching. It is in respect of laying this, that the names of the twelve apostles (not of St. Peter only) were equally inscribed on the twelve foundations of the city of God, Rev. xxi, 14. The gates of hell - As gates and walls were the strength of cities, and as courts of judicature were held in their gates, this phrase properly signifies the power and policy of Satan and his instruments. Shall not prevail against it - Not against the Church universal, so as to destroy it. And they never did. There hath been a small remnant in all ages.

I will give thee the keys of the kingdom of heaven — Indeed not to him alone, (for they were equally given to all the apostles at the same time, John xx, 21, 22, 23;) but to him were first given the keys both of doctrine and discipline. He first, after our Lord's resurrection, exercised the apostleship, Acts i, 15. And he first by preaching opened the kingdom of heaven, both to the Jews, Acts ii, , and to the Gentiles, Acts x, . Under the term of binding and loosing are contained all those acts of discipline which Peter and his brethren performed as apostles: and undoubtedly what they thus performed on earth, God confirmed in heaven. Matt. xviii, 18.

Then charged he his disciples to tell no one that he was the Christ. Jesus himself had not said it expressly even to his apostles, but left them to infer it from his doctrine and miracles. Neither was it proper the apostles should say this openly, before that grand proof of it, his resurrection. If they had, they who believed them would the more earnestly have sought to take and make him a king: and they who did not believe them would the more vehemently have rejected and opposed such a Messiah.

glossa.text: *Into the parts of Caesarea Philippi.* This is the place where the Jordan rises at the foot of Lebanon, out of Jor and Dan, two springs. *That men say he is.* They are men who speak of the Son of man: for they are gods who understand the Godhead. *The Son of man?* The Lord professes of himself the lowliness of his humanity, while the disciples understand his Godhead.

*Some, John the Baptist.* So they could err about Elias or about the rest of the others, as Herod erred about John when he said: *John, whom I beheaded, is risen from the dead: and therefore mighty works are wrought in him ((Marc. VI))* . Therefore he wills that their errors be set forth, so that, these being driven off, the disciples may bring forth the truth, not out of the opinion of the common people, but out of the Lord's revelation.

*Simon Peter answering.* Therefore one answers, and to one answer is made on behalf of all, that unity may be kept in all. *Of the living God.* For a distinction from the false gods, which the Gentiles set up for themselves either out of dead men or out of sensible matter.

*Barjona.* Well is he the son of the dove, because he followed the Lord with a devout simplicity, or because he was full of spiritual grace. He is called the son of the Holy Spirit, who was shown in the dove, by him whom he had called the Son of the living God, and to the son of the dove the Father reveals, because the operation of the Father and of the Son with the Holy Spirit is one. He reveals, I say, the mystery of faith, because flesh and blood could not reveal it, that is, men puffed up with carnal wisdom, who are not sons of the dove, and therefore strangers to the wisdom of the Spirit; of whom above: *Others John the Baptist, and others Elias,* etc.

*Thou art.* I do not say, thou shalt be called, but thou art Peter, for the strength of thy faith and the constancy of thy confession. *Peter.* From me, the Rock, yet so that I keep for myself the dignity of the foundation: thou shalt set clean stones upon me, and shalt cast away the leprous.

Just as light and the other names, as: *You are the salt of the earth,* were allotted to the apostles by the Lord, so to Simon he gave from himself the name of Peter.

*And the gates.* The gates of hell are sins, threats, blandishments, heresies, by which the weak rush into death, who are to be believed to have built the house of their profession not truly upon the rock, but upon the sand, that is, not to follow Christ with a simple and true intention, but to have put forward the habit for some earthly cause. For he who receives the faith of Christ in the inmost love of the heart easily overcomes whatever assails him from without.

*And whatsoever thou shalt bind.* That is, whomsoever thou shalt have adjudged to eternal punishments as persisting in his sins, or whomsoever thou shalt have absolved as humble and truly penitent, so shall it be also in heaven.

*And whatsoever thou shalt bind upon earth. ((HIER.))* The other apostles have indeed the same judicial power, to whom after the resurrection he says: *Receive ye the Holy Spirit ((Joan. XX))*, etc., *as far as* whence in Leviticus the lepers are bidden to show themselves to the priests, whom the priests do not make lepers, but discern who are clean or unclean, so also here.

*That they should tell no man,* etc. Above he commands them to preach his coming, here that they should not say that he is Jesus. But it is one thing to preach Christ, which is a common name of dignity: another to preach Jesus, which is the Saviour's own name. As if he said: It does not profit that my majesty be publicly preached to the peoples, who are to see me suffer many things, which will be lawful only then, when the resurrection shall have shown the power of the Godhead. *Jesus Christ.* The Saviour: lest they should be scandalized in him whom a little after they are to see spat upon and crucified.

echoes.text: “‘If his offering is a burnt offering from the herd, he shall offer a male without defect. He shall offer it at the door of the Tent of Meeting, that he may be accepted before Yahweh. He shall lay his hand on the head of the burnt offering, and it shall be accepted for him to make atonement for him.
echoes.note: "Present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God" reuses the technical cultic vocabulary of the burnt offering, which must be presented/brought 'acceptable before the LORD' (LXX dekton). Paul figurally transposes the Levitical offering from animal victim to the embodied self.

echoes.text: For you don’t delight in sacrifice, or else I would give it. You have no pleasure in burnt offering. The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit. A broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise.
echoes.note: The Psalm's claim that God does not delight in animal sacrifice but in 'a broken spirit' anticipates Paul's redefinition of true worship (logike latreia) as the offering of the whole self rather than the slain victim.

echoes.text: Samuel said, “Has Yahweh as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of Yahweh? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams.
echoes.note: 'To obey is better than sacrifice' belongs to the prophetic stream that internalizes and ethicizes cult; Paul's 'reasonable/spiritual service' redirects sacrifice toward obedient self-presentation in the same key.

echoes.text: I will also give you a new heart, and I will put a new spirit within you; and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh.
echoes.note: The promise of a 'new heart and a new spirit' stands behind 'be transformed by the renewing of your mind'; the eschatological interior renewal of the prophets is here applied to the believing community.

echoes.text: For I desire mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.
echoes.note: 'I desire mercy and not sacrifice' is part of the prophetic critique that grounds Paul's reframing of worship as embodied, merciful obedience rather than ritual offering.

echoes.text: How shall I come before Yahweh, and bow myself before the exalted God? Shall I come before him with burnt offerings, with calves a year old? Will Yahweh be pleased with thousands of rams? With tens of thousands of rivers of oil? Shall I give my firstborn for my disobedience? The fruit of my body for the sin of my soul? He has shown you, O man, what is good. What does Yahweh require of you, but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?
echoes.note: Micah's rhetorical rejection of burnt offerings in favor of doing justice and walking humbly parallels Paul's contrast between cultic sacrifice and 'living sacrifice' as the true service God requires.

echoes.text: But this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, says Yahweh: I will put my law in their inward parts, and in their heart will I write it; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people:
echoes.note: The new-covenant law written on the heart/mind (LXX dianoia) coheres with the 'renewing of the mind' that enables one to discern God's will; faint verbal contact via mind/heart-renewal.

echoes.text: For this commandment which I command you this day is not too hard for you or too distant. It is not in heaven, that you should say, “Who will go up for us to heaven, and bring it to us, and proclaim it to us, that we may do it?” Neither is it beyond the sea, that you should say, “Who will go over the sea for us, and bring it to us, and proclaim it to us, that we may do it?” But the word is very near to you, in your mouth and in your heart, that you may do […]
echoes.note: Discerning and doing 'the good and acceptable and perfect will of God' echoes Deuteronomy's insistence that God's commandment is knowable and doable, internalized in heart and mouth — a theme Paul invokes nearby in Romans 10.

echoes.text: Don’t be wise in your own eyes. Fear Yahweh, and depart from evil.
echoes.note: 'Not to think of himself more highly than he ought' draws on the wisdom warning 'Be not wise in your own eyes'; the same maxim returns explicitly at 12:16, framing the pericope's call to sober self-estimation.

echoes.text: Do you see a man wise in his own eyes? There is more hope for a fool than for him.
echoes.note: 'Do you see a man wise in his own conceit? There is more hope for a fool' supplies the proverbial backdrop for Paul's exhortation against inflated self-regard ('think reasonably').

echoes.text: Pride is hateful before the Lord and before men; And in the judgement of both will unrighteousness err.
echoes.note: Sirach's wisdom that 'pride is hateful before the Lord and before men' is a Second Temple parallel to Paul's call not to over-rate oneself but to measure by the faith God apportions.
