echoes.text: I will lay the key of the house of David on his shoulder. He will open, and no one will shut. He will shut, and no one will open.
echoes.note: 'I will give you the keys of the Kingdom of Heaven... bind... loose' draws on the Eliakim oracle: 'I will place on his shoulder the key of the house of David; he shall open and none shut, shut and none open.' The key-of-stewardship granting authority to admit and exclude is the controlling image. Strong verbal and conceptual borrowing.

echoes.text: Have the gates of death been revealed to you? Or have you seen the gates of the shadow of death?
echoes.note: 'The gates of Hades will not prevail' echoes 'Have the gates of death been revealed to you?' — the underworld as a fortified city whose gates symbolize the realm and power of death. Verbal touchpoint ('gates' of death/Hades).

echoes.text: Have mercy on me, Yahweh. See my affliction by those who hate me, and lift me up from the gates of death;
echoes.note: 'You who lift me up from the gates of death' supplies the same 'gates of death/Hades' idiom; deliverance from death's gates is precisely what Jesus' resurrection-grounded assembly will enjoy. Reinforces Job 38:17.

echoes.text: I said, “In the middle of my life I go into the gates of Sheol. I am deprived of the residue of my years.”
echoes.note: Hezekiah's 'I shall go through the gates of Sheol' offers another close instance of the 'gates of the underworld' figure standing behind 'gates of Hades.'

echoes.text: For who is there of all flesh, that has heard the voice of the living God speaking out of the midst of the fire, as we have, and lived?
echoes.note: Peter's confession of Jesus as 'the Son of the living God' employs the covenant title 'the living God,' contrasting Israel's God with lifeless idols. The epithet recurs across the OT and grounds the confession in covenant monotheism.

echoes.text: Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of Yahweh comes.
echoes.note: The popular identification of Jesus with Elijah ('some say... Elijah') depends on Malachi's promise that Elijah would return before the day of the LORD, an expectation Matthew engages elsewhere (11:14; 17:10-13).

echoes.text: Yet the number of the children of Israel will be as the sand of the sea, which can’t be measured nor numbered; and it will come to pass that, in the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ they will be called ‘sons of the living God.’
echoes.note: 'Sons of the living God' supplies the specific collocation 'living God' with sonship language that Peter's title brings together. Faint verbal overlap.

echoes.text: “Listen to me, you who follow after righteousness, you who seek Yahweh: look to the rock you were cut from, and to the hold of the pit you were dug from. Look to Abraham your father, and to Sarah who bore you; for when he was but one I called him, and I blessed him, and made him many.
echoes.note: 'On this rock I will build' may play on the 'rock from which you were hewn' (Abraham) imagery for the founding of the people of God on a chosen progenitor. Disputed; rock-foundation imagery is diffuse.

echoes.text: “Before I formed you in the belly, I knew you. Before you came out of the womb, I sanctified you. I have appointed you a prophet to the nations.”
echoes.note: Jeremiah being named among the guesses for Jesus' identity reflects his stature as the suffering, rejected prophet of judgment on Jerusalem; the allusion is to Jeremiah as a prophetic type rather than a specific text. Faint.

turn.trap: Becomes a jurisdictional argument about Peter and papal authority (missing the pastoral point), or a private orthodoxy quiz — missing that the confession is revealed to Peter, not achieved by him: he didn't reason his way there.
turn.hinge: The mouth that just spoke the truest thing anyone in the Gospel has said will, six verses later, be called "Satan" for refusing the cross. The rock and the stumbling-block are the same man in the same conversation.

doors.landing: Whom do men say, whom do you say
doors.claim: The crowd's guesses — John, Elijah, a prophet — are all half-true and none of them enough; the question turns from public opinion to personal confession.

witnesses.author: Jerome
witnesses.reading: Beautifully is the question put, 'Whom do men say that the Son of Man is?' For they who speak of the Son of Man, are men.

witnesses.author: John Chrysostom
witnesses.reading: He says not, Whom do the Scribes and Pharisees say that I am? but, Whom do men say that I am? searching into the minds of the common people... and by a second question invites them to higher thoughts.

doors.say: Every crowd has an opinion about Jesus, and none of them are quite the truth — the question isn't settled until it's asked of you.
doors.do: Have them write down what "people say" about Jesus today, then set it aside and answer the question themselves.

doors.claim: Peter did not reason his way to the confession — flesh and blood did not reveal it, the Father did. The church's foundation is a gift received, not a conclusion argued.

witnesses.author: Hilary of Poitiers
witnesses.reading: This confession of Peter met a worthy reward, for that he had seen the Son of God in the man... to have looked and to have seen beyond human sight is matter of praise.

witnesses.author: Augustine
witnesses.reading: It was on him, as on a rock, that the Church was built. But I know that since that I have often explained... that this rock was Christ.

doors.say: Peter didn't figure this out — it was shown to him. What you know rightly about Jesus was given to you, not earned by you.
doors.do: Ask them to name one true thing about Jesus they now hold that they once could not have reasoned their way to.

doors.landing: Gates of hell, keys of heaven
doors.claim: The promise is not a grant of institutional power but authority over the real enemy — sin and the grave, opened by binding and loosing in Christ's name.

witnesses.author: Origen
witnesses.reading: Every spiritual sin is a gate of hell, to which are opposed the gates of righteousness.

witnesses.author: Origen
witnesses.reading: Let him then be without blame who binds or looses another, that he may be found worthy to bind or loose in heaven.

doors.say: The keys were never about who's in charge — they're about what actually holds people captive, and what sets them free.
doors.do: Have them name a sin they've watched "bind" someone, and pray specifically for its loosing this week.

semicontinuous.gravity: Pharaoh's decree to kill every Hebrew boy is undone by two midwives who fear God more than the king (Exodus 1-2); the Psalm sings of a soul escaped like a bird from the snare; Paul urges "be transformed by the renewing of your mind," not conformed to the age (Romans 12); and Jesus asks the question that decides everything: "Who do you say that I am?" The nerve: the answer that saves comes not from majority opinion but from a mind renewed enough to see past the crowd's guesses.

synthesis.convergence: Two midwives defy an empire's decree out of fear of God, not fear of Pharaoh (Exodus 1); Paul insists the renewed mind stops being conformed to its age (Romans 12); Peter's confession only lands because he has stopped repeating what "men" say and heard what the Father reveals. Every text asks whose voice actually governs you — the empire's, the crowd's, or the one revealed from above.
synthesis.claim: The crowd's opinion of Jesus is not nothing, but it will never be enough — until you say who he is for yourself.
synthesis.here: For a congregation absorbing every hot take about Jesus from the culture around them, the move is Peter's: stop reciting what everyone else says, and answer the question put to you directly.

turn.subtract: Three landings — from crowd-opinion to confession, the gift of revelation, or the real stakes of the keys. Choose one. A fourth door — Peter as rock of papal authority — is deliberately not opened here: it's ecumenically loaded, and Augustine's own later clarification (above) already complicates a simple reading. Raise it only if directly asked.
